clue.text: Provenance of J. B. Morton's Dr Strabismus (Whom God Preserve)

definitions.text: Provenance of J. B. Morton's Dr Strabismus (Whom God Preserve)

parts.words: Provenance of J. B. Morton's Dr Strabismus (Whom God Preserve)
parts.note: Beachcomber's comic sage was always styled as hailing from a Dutch university city

explanation.surface: A question of where a famous comic newspaper character came from.
explanation.walkthrough: J. B. Morton wrote the Beachcomber column in the Daily Express; his recurring figure was Dr Strabismus (Whom God Preserve) of a city in the Netherlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch city is the place named in the character's full mock-grand title.

clue.text: Worried, unlike Marryat's young officer

parts.note: un- is the negating prefix, making the following name its opposite
Captain Marryat's novel is Mr Midshipman Easy, about a young naval officer

explanation.surface: Someone anxious, in contrast to a carefree fictional midshipman.
explanation.walkthrough: Frederick Marryat wrote the naval novel Mr Midshipman Easy; a midshipman is a junior officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being anxious and ill at ease is the same as being worried.

clue.text: Byron wondered if our carcases were worth it

definitions.text: Byron wondered if our carcases were worth it

parts.words: Byron wondered if our carcases were worth it
parts.note: echoes Byron's line asking whether our dead bodies are worth lifting up again at the Resurrection

explanation.surface: A poet doubts whether human bodies deserve some effort.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron, in his Vision of Judgment, wonders whether our carcases are worth the effort of resurrection; the clue gives no letter count.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifting the dead up again is the act Byron questioned, the bringing back of bodies.

clue.text: Sudden seizure of power somehow due to pact

indicators.note: somehow says the letters are put together in some new way

explanation.surface: A government is overthrown in a way blamed on some treaty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges the letters of DUE TO PACT.
explanation.definitionFit: A French term for an abrupt, often military, overthrow of a government.

clue.text: At Bayreuth I recast a few verses from arty habitué

indicators.note: recast means cast again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone at the Wagner festival reworks poems picked up from an artistic regular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recast' rearranges AT BAYREUTH I; 'arty habitué' is a second set of the same letters. FitzGerald's version of Omar Khayyam is a set of quatrains.
explanation.definitionFit: FitzGerald's famous Persian collection is a sequence of short quatrains.

clue.text: Some informal, thus accessible economist

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An economist whose writing is casual and so easy to read.
explanation.walkthrough: The economist sits openly inside the clue's words, so he is readily got at.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Robert Malthus was the English political economist of population theory, and here he is easy to reach in the text.

clue.text: Ivy Compton-Burnett's had wives, but Hemingway's were without women

definitions.meaning: Compton-Burnett's novel title pairs males with wives
Hemingway's story collection title puts males without women

explanation.surface: Contrasting the married males of one author with the lonely ones of another.
explanation.definitionFit: Both book titles begin with the plural word for adult males: Men and Wives, and Men Without Women.

clue.text: Snake-woman returns in search of claim allowance

indicators.note: returns means the run of letters comes back, read in reverse
in search of says the letters are to be looked for inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A monstrous creature goes back looking for an insurance payout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in search of' finds AIMAL inside 'claim allowance' and 'returns' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth and Keats's poem, the creature is a serpent with a woman's form.

clue.text: Miss Vane, author and creation of

definitions.text: Miss Vane, author and creation of

parts.words: Miss Vane, author and creation of
parts.note: the blank points to 17 across, whose detective-story heroine is herself a mystery novelist

explanation.surface: A writer character created by the crime novelist at 17 across.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank stands for 17 across, Dorothy L Sayers, whose heroine Harriet Vane writes detective novels and marries Lord Peter Wimsey.
explanation.definitionFit: Her first name is the given name of the heroine of Strong Poison and Gaudy Night.

clue.text: Little girl in Germany conceals reclusive novelist

parts.note: Sal is a short pet form of the girl's name Sally

explanation.surface: A small girl abroad hides a writer who shuns the public.
explanation.walkthrough: J. D. Salinger, author of The Catcher in the Rye, famously withdrew from public life.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of The Catcher in the Rye spent decades as a famous hermit in New Hampshire.

clue.text: Marius, eg

parts.note: Walter Pater's novel has the title Marius the..., so its hero is an example of a follower of a Greek philosophy

explanation.surface: A Roman name given as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter Pater's novel is Marius the Epicurean.
explanation.definitionFit: Pater's hero follows the pleasure-seeking philosophy of Epicurus.

clue.text: Proustian fungoid fiddler ()

parts.note: the violinist in Proust's novel shares his surname with an edible honeycombed mushroom

explanation.surface: A mushroom-like violinist from a French novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Morel is the violinist in A la recherche du temps perdu; the morel is a prized wild mushroom, hence 'fungoid'.
explanation.definitionFit: The violinist in Proust shares a surname with a prized edible wild mushroom.

clue.text: Noticed what George Smiley did ()

definitions.meaning: le Carre's George Smiley was an intelligence officer, so he worked in espionage

explanation.surface: Observing le Carre's famous intelligence officer at work.
explanation.definitionFit: Catching sight of something is spotting it, and a secret agent's work is espionage.

clue.text: "Again the horns were fill'd by all / And -s shook the hall" (George Colman)

definitions.text: "Again the horns were fill'd by all / And -s shook the hall" (George Colman)

parts.words: "Again the horns were fill'd by all / And -s shook the hall" (George Colman)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap to fill: the plural noun for loud howling cries that echo in a hall

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-gap quotation from a Georgian playwright's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash in the quotation is the missing word, given in the singular as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud wailing or howling is the sound that fills the hall in Colman's lines.

clue.text: Like Sylvia Ashton-Warner's eponymous woman — perhaps because not cultivated?

definitions.meaning: Ashton-Warner's novel Spinster is named after an unmarried woman
husband is an old verb for tilling land, so land never tilled is described this way

explanation.surface: A novel's single heroine is linked to fields left untended.
explanation.walkthrough: Husbandry means farming, so the word works for both an unmarried woman and untilled land.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinster has no spouse, and an untended field has had no farming care.

clue.text: "I'd much rather lie in a hot bath reading and sucking sweets" (Dylan Thomas)

definitions.text: "I'd much rather lie in a hot bath reading and sucking sweets" (Dylan Thomas)

parts.words: "I'd much rather lie in a hot bath reading and sucking sweets" (Dylan Thomas)
parts.note: a quotation with the name of the author Thomas liked to read left out

explanation.surface: Dylan Thomas confesses his idea of a perfect evening's indulgence.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas's line runs 'reading Agatha Christie and sucking sweets'; the missing words are the crime writer's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The queen of detective fiction is the writer Thomas preferred to read in the bath.

clue.text: Styli slid out of control, describing poets like Tennyson

indicators.note: out of control means running wild, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Pens slip across the page while describing Victorian poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of control' rearranges STYLI SLID. Tennyson wrote Idylls of the King.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers of pastoral or romantic narrative poems, as in Tennyson's Idylls of the King.

clue.text: Gilpin's anniversary trysting-place

parts.note: Cowper's John Gilpin planned to meet his wife for their wedding anniversary at an inn at the Bell in a north London town

explanation.surface: Where a comic hero meant to meet his wife on their wedding anniversary.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cowper's ballad John Gilpin, he arranges to dine at the Bell at Edmonton, then north of London, but his horse bolts past it.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad's planned anniversary dinner was at the Bell inn in this north London town.

clue.text: Crime writer unfortunately so deathly (sorry)

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A mystery novelist apologises for something deadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges SO DEATHLY with SORRY.
explanation.definitionFit: She wrote the Lord Peter Wimsey detective novels.

clue.text: Canadian novelist, very well off (and only half toiler)

parts.note: very well off means wealthy

indicators.note: only half says to keep just the back three letters of the six-letter word

explanation.surface: A wealthy Canadian author who works only part-time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only half' takes the last half of TOILER, giving LER. Mordecai Richler wrote The Apprenticeship of Duddy Kravitz.
explanation.definitionFit: Mordecai Richler was a Montreal-born writer of comic novels.

clue.text: Price paid to English children's writer

parts.note: a price paid for release of a captive is a ransom

explanation.surface: Money handed over to an author of books for the young.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ransome wrote Swallows and Amazons.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ransome wrote the Swallows and Amazons sailing stories for young readers.

clue.text: Dramatist, we hear, was dramatist's subject

indicators.note: we hear says the name is spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: Samuel Beckett was the dramatist of Waiting for Godot

explanation.surface: A playwright is himself the topic of another playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Becket, the murdered archbishop, is the subject of plays by Tennyson, Eliot and Anouilh.
explanation.definitionFit: The martyred archbishop of Canterbury was the hero of Anouilh's and Tennyson's plays.

clue.text: It might be banned, say, in more downmarket sense

definitions.text: It might be banned, say, in more downmarket sense

parts.words: It might be banned, say, in more downmarket sense
parts.note: banned sounds like band, and a downmarket word for a large group of players is a band

explanation.surface: Something that could be prohibited in a cruder way of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banned' said aloud is 'band', a humbler word for a large ensemble of musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: A symphonic body of players can be called, more casually, a band.

clue.text: Proven nuisance value of required reading conceals boredom

indicators.note: conceals says the letters lie hidden inside the words before it

parts.words: Proven nuisance value of required reading

explanation.surface: A tedious book on a reading list hides a sense of weariness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conceals' finds the run inside 'Proven nuisance'.
explanation.definitionFit: A French loan word for listless weariness and dissatisfaction.

clue.text: Sharp instrument for Thackeray's surgeon

definitions.meaning: a pointed weapon or small surgical blade
Thackeray names a surgeon in his fiction with this surname

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist's doctor with a cutting tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A long pointed spear, or a verb for cutting open, shared with a Thackeray doctor's surname.

clue.text: Used in mortal onset, by "The Windhover", possibly ?

definitions.text: Used in mortal onset, by "The Windhover", possibly ?

indicators.note: in says the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A hawk's deadly swoop, from Hopkins's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' finds the claw hidden in 'mortal onset'. Hopkins's The Windhover is a kestrel, a bird of prey that strikes with its claws.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird of prey's claw is what it strikes with as it swoops on its prey.

clue.text: Clothing item, perhaps, associated with violets in song staged by Don Adriano de Armado

definitions.text: Clothing item, perhaps, associated with violets in song staged by Don Adriano de Armado

parts.words: Clothing item, perhaps, associated with violets in song staged by Don Adriano de Armado
parts.note: the spring song in Love's Labour's Lost names a meadow flower beside violets, and its name sounds like a woman's garment

explanation.surface: A garment mentioned in a Shakespearean song.
explanation.walkthrough: Armado presents the closing song of Love's Labour's Lost: 'When daisies pied and violets blue, / And lady-smocks all silver-white'.
explanation.definitionFit: The cuckoo flower, a pale meadow plant, appears beside violets in Shakespeare's spring song.

clue.text: Heraldic flower starts literary interest somehow

indicators.note: starts points to the opening letter of each of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A flower in a coat of arms sparks an interest in books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' takes the first letters of 'literary interest somehow'. A lis is the fleur-de-lis.
explanation.definitionFit: The French lily of heraldry, as in fleur-de-lis.

clue.text: Nymphs, before seen in terrible rows

indicators.note: seen in places one piece within the other
terrible says the noisy word's letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: rows, rhyming with cows, are noisy quarrels or dins
ere is a poetic word for before

explanation.surface: Sea spirits glimpsed earlier amid dreadful arguments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' turns DINS into NIDS and 'seen in' puts ERE inside it after the N.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea maidens of Greek myth, daughters of Nereus.

clue.text: Harold Robins's novel a bit of a comedown from Coleridge's vision

definitions.text: Harold Robins's novel a bit of a comedown from Coleridge's vision

parts.words: Harold Robins's novel a bit of a comedown from Coleridge's vision
parts.note: Harold Robbins's novel takes its title from a fall from Kubla Khan's pleasure-dome site

explanation.surface: A popular novelist's title is a drop in quality from a Romantic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Robbins wrote Descent from Xanadu; Xanadu is the visionary setting of Coleridge's Kubla Khan.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedown is a fall or drop, the first word of the Robbins title.
